subject: physics

items.q: A lamp has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 2.5 A through it. What is the power transfer in the lamp?
items.why: The most-practised electrical equation is V = I R, which is usually rearranged by dividing, so dividing becomes the default move. P = V I is a product, not a ratio. Dividing V by I would give the resistance in ohms, not a power in watts.

items.q: A current of 3.0 A passes through a resistor of resistance 5.0 Ω. What is the power transfer in the resistor?
items.why: 15 W is what V = I R produces, and the familiar shape of that equation overwrites the unfamiliar squared term. I R gives a potential difference in volts, not a power in watts. Square the current first, then multiply by the resistance.

items.q: Which row gives the correct unit for every quantity in the equation P = I² R?
items.correct: power in watts, current in amperes, resistance in ohms
items.misconception: power in joules, current in amperes, resistance in ohms
items.why: The only electrical unit students meet on real appliances is the watt, so it becomes their default energy unit. The watt measures the rate of transfer. The answer to any E = P t or E = Q V calculation is in joules.
items.random_wrong: power in watts, current in coulombs, resistance in ohms

items.q: The potential difference across a fixed resistor is doubled. What happens to the power transfer in the resistor?
items.correct: The power becomes four times larger
items.misconception: The power becomes exactly twice as large
items.why: Students read P = V I as if only V changes, holding I fixed, because I is a separate symbol on the page. Check whether the other quantity changes too. For a fixed resistance, doubling V doubles I, so P = V I gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the power.
items.random_wrong: The power stays exactly the same value

items.q: The specification states that work is done when charge flows in a circuit. What does this mean?
items.correct: Energy is transferred as charge is pushed through the components
items.misconception: Charge is gradually used up as it goes round the circuit
items.why: Batteries do go flat, and students attach that running-out to the charge rather than to the energy stored chemically. Separate the two ideas: the same charge circulates continuously, while energy is transferred from the supply to the components as work is done.
items.random_wrong: Work is done only when part of the circuit actually moves

items.q: An electric heater has a power of 2000 W and is switched on for 3.0 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?
items.why: The question states the time in minutes, and students substitute the number they are shown without checking the unit. In E = P t, t must be in seconds, s. Convert minutes and hours to seconds before substituting.

items.q: A current of 0.50 A flows for 600 s through a component with a potential difference of 12 V across it. How much energy is transferred?
items.why: Power and energy are both 'how much' quantities in everyday speech, and the label is the only number the student is given. Read the watt as 'joules every second'. A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J each second, so you must multiply by the number of seconds to get the energy.

items.q: Which row gives the correct unit for every quantity in the equation E = Q V?
items.correct: E in joules, Q in coulombs, V in volts
items.misconception: E in joules, Q in amperes, V in volts
items.why: Current and charge are both about 'electricity moving', and Q appears in Q = I t alongside current. Charge flow is in coulombs; current is in amperes. If you are given a current and a time, first find Q = I t, then use E = Q V.
items.random_wrong: E in watts, Q in coulombs, V in volts

items.q: A food mixer is plugged into the ac mains and switched on. Which statement best describes the useful energy transfer?
items.correct: Energy is transferred electrically to a kinetic energy store
items.misconception: Energy is transferred electrically to a chemical energy store
items.why: Batteries are introduced first and do involve chemical stores, so students generalise the idea to every electrical supply. Describe the pathway, not the socket: energy is transferred electrically from the supply to the store in the appliance. Only the battery itself holds a chemical store.
items.random_wrong: Energy is transferred by heating to a kinetic energy store

items.q: A cordless drill runs from a rechargeable battery. An identical mains drill runs from the ac mains. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Both drills transfer energy electrically to a kinetic store
items.misconception: Only the mains drill transfers energy electrically to a motor
items.why: Mains appliances are described using the word electricity far more often, so the battery route feels like a different phenomenon. The supply differs, the transfer does not. In both cases the supply does electrical work on the charge flowing through the motor.
items.random_wrong: The battery drill uses ac and the mains drill uses dc supply

items.q: Appliance A has a power of 1200 W and is used for 5.0 minutes. Appliance B has a power of 400 W and is used for 20 minutes. Which transfers more energy?
items.correct: B, because it transfers 480 000 J and A only 360 000 J
items.misconception: A, because its power rating is three times that of B
items.why: Power rating is the number students are shown most often, so it becomes the only variable they attend to. Always compute E = P t for each appliance. A 400 W appliance run for 20 minutes transfers more energy than a 1200 W appliance run for 5 minutes.
items.random_wrong: B, because time alone decides the energy transferred

items.q: A 900 W microwave oven and a 60 W lamp are each switched on for exactly 1.0 minute. Which statement about the energy transferred is correct?
items.correct: The microwave transfers 54 000 J and the lamp 3600 J
items.misconception: The microwave transfers 900 J and the lamp only 60 J
items.why: Power and energy are both 'how much' quantities in everyday speech, and the label is the only number the student is given. Read the watt as 'joules every second'. A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J each second, so you must multiply by the number of seconds to get the energy.
items.random_wrong: The microwave transfers 54 000 W and the lamp 3600 W

items.q: What is the National Grid?
items.correct: A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers
items.misconception: A system of power stations that generates all of the country's electricity
items.why: News reports talk about the grid supplying the country, which sounds like the grid is the source. Power stations generate; the grid transfers. The grid's parts are cables and transformers, not generators.
items.random_wrong: A network of cables that stores electricity until consumers need it

items.q: Which statement correctly describes where the transformers are used in the National Grid?
items.correct: Step-up transformers near power stations, step-down near consumers
items.misconception: Step-down transformers near power stations, step-up near homes
items.why: Students associate 'up' with going up the pylons towards the house at the end of the journey, rather than with the potential difference. The words describe the potential difference, not position or direction of travel. Homes need a much lower pd, so the last transformer must step down.
items.random_wrong: Step-up transformers at both ends of the transmission cables

items.q: Why does transferring electrical power at a very high potential difference make the National Grid an efficient way to transfer energy?
items.correct: The current is smaller, so less energy is wasted heating the cables
items.misconception: The current is larger, so more energy reaches the consumers quickly
items.why: Bigger is assumed to be better for everything, and current is the quantity students most associate with 'how much electricity'. P = V I: at fixed power, raising V must lower I. The saving comes from the smaller current, through P = I² R.
items.random_wrong: The resistance of the cables is reduced by the high potential difference

items.q: A transmission cable has a resistance of 4.0 Ω and carries a current of 100 A. What power is wasted heating the cable?
items.why: The pattern 'current times resistance' is heavily practised through V = I R and is applied here without checking the equation. For wasted power use P = I² R and square the current first. The answer 400 would be a potential difference in volts.

items.q: The same electrical power is transmitted at ten times the potential difference, so the current in the cables falls to one tenth. What happens to the power wasted in the cables?
items.correct: It falls to one hundredth
items.misconception: It falls to one tenth
items.why: Students assume proportionality by default and do not notice that the square changes the scaling factor. Scale the squared quantity: (1/10)² = 1/100. Halving the current quarters the wasted power, and so on.
items.random_wrong: It falls to a thousandth

items.q: A motor connected to a 12 V supply transfers 18 000 J of energy in 60 s. What is the current through the motor?
items.why: Power and energy are both 'how much' quantities in everyday speech, and the label is the only number the student is given. Read the watt as 'joules every second'. A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J each second, so you must multiply by the number of seconds to get the energy.

items.q: A charge of 45 C flows through a lamp and 540 J of energy is transferred. What is the potential difference across the lamp?
items.why: Students recall that the equation involves a product and multiply the two numbers they are given without rearranging first. Write the equation, identify which symbol is unknown, then rearrange. Only the two quantities on the right are multiplied together.

items.q: An electric kettle is connected to the ac mains and boils some water. Which statement describes the main energy transfer?
items.correct: Energy is transferred electrically to the water's thermal store
items.misconception: Energy is transferred electrically into the kettle's kinetic store
items.why: Students know current warms wires, so heating becomes the mechanism they reach for in every electrical device. Name the pathway correctly: the transfer to a motor is electrical, and the useful store filled is kinetic. Heating in the wires is a wasteful side effect.
items.random_wrong: Energy stored chemically in the mains is transferred to the water

items.q: Which change would exactly double the energy an appliance transfers?
items.correct: Keep the power the same and double the time it is on
items.misconception: Double the power and halve the time it is switched on
items.why: Power rating is the number students are shown most often, so it becomes the only variable they attend to. Always compute E = P t for each appliance. A 400 W appliance run for 20 minutes transfers more energy than a 1200 W appliance run for 5 minutes.
items.random_wrong: Halve the power and keep the time it is on the same

items.q: Which statement about the National Grid is correct?
items.correct: It transfers electrical power from power stations to consumers
items.misconception: It generates the electrical power that consumers use
items.why: News reports talk about the grid supplying the country, which sounds like the grid is the source. Power stations generate; the grid transfers. The grid's parts are cables and transformers, not generators.
items.random_wrong: It stores electrical power until consumers switch things on

items.q: A hairdryer is rated at 1800 W and runs from a 230 V mains supply. What current does it take, and how much energy does it transfer in 2.0 minutes?
items.why: The most-practised electrical equation is V = I R, which is usually rearranged by dividing, so dividing becomes the default move. P = V I is a product, not a ratio. Dividing V by I would give the resistance in ohms, not a power in watts.

items.q: Which quantity is measured in coulombs?
items.correct: The flow of charge past a point
items.misconception: The current in a circuit branch
items.why: Both quantities are introduced together and both are described using the word charge. One ampere is one coulomb passing each second. The coulomb measures how much charge; the ampere measures how fast it passes.
items.random_wrong: The energy a device transfers

items.q: Does the power of a fixed resistor change if the supply is changed?
items.correct: Yes. Resistance is fixed, but the current and potential difference change, so the power changes.
items.misconception: Because the resistance of the resistor does not change, its power cannot change either.
items.why: Students treat every property printed on a component as a fixed characteristic of that component, including the power. Resistance is a property of the component; power depends on how hard the circuit drives it, through P = V I or P = I² R.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In P = V I, does anything need squaring?
items.correct: No. Only P = I² R contains a square, and it is the current that is squared.
items.misconception: You square the current in P = V I as well, so 12 V and 2.5 A give 12 × 2.5² = 75 W.
items.why: The two power equations are learned together and the square migrates from one to the other. Match the equation to the quantities you are given: pd and current means P = V I with no square; current and resistance means P = I² R with the current squared.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In P = I² R, which quantity is squared?
items.correct: The current is squared. The resistance is not.
items.misconception: The resistance is squared, so a 3.0 A current in a 5.0 Ω resistor gives 3.0 × 5.0² = 75 W.
items.why: The superscript is read as belonging to the whole right-hand side rather than to the symbol it sits on. The index sits on I alone. Write the substitution as (3.0)² × 5.0 so the square is unmistakably attached to the current.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is work done in a circuit even though nothing visibly moves?
items.correct: Yes. Work is done when charge flows in a circuit, and that work is the energy transferred electrically.
items.misconception: Work is only done when an object moves, so no work is done in a circuit with no moving parts.
items.why: Work is first met as force × distance with a visibly moving object, so an invisible flow of charge does not look like work. Charge moving through a potential difference is movement. The supply does work on the charge, which is why E = Q V gives an energy in joules.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do you combine power and time to find energy?
items.correct: Multiply them: energy transferred = power × time, E = P t.
items.misconception: You divide the power by the time, so 2000 W over 180 s gives about 11 J.
items.why: Power is often described as 'energy per second', and the word per makes students divide by the time instead of multiplying. Power per second means energy each second, so multiply by the number of seconds. Dividing gives a quantity with no physical meaning here.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A charge of 300 C flows through a lamp. Is 300 J transferred?
items.correct: No. The energy also depends on the potential difference: E = Q V, so at 12 V the transfer is 3600 J.
items.misconception: The charge flow is the energy transferred, so 300 C means 300 J.
items.why: Both are single numbers describing 'how much has gone through', so students treat them as the same quantity in different clothes. Charge is what flows; energy is what the charge delivers. Multiply the charge by the potential difference it moves through.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a battery supply ac or dc, and what about the mains?
items.correct: A battery supplies direct current; the mains supplies alternating current, which is why the specification says 'ac mains'.
items.misconception: Batteries give ac because the charge keeps moving, and the mains gives dc because it is steady.
items.why: The words alternating and direct are not connected to anything the student can see, so the labels get swapped. Link 'ac' to the mains socket and 'dc' to the battery. Both can drive the same appliance and bring about the same energy transfer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does raising the potential difference change the resistance of the cables?
items.correct: No. The cable resistance is unchanged; it is the current that falls, and the wasted power falls with the square of the current.
items.misconception: A high potential difference lowers the resistance of the transmission cables, so less energy is wasted.
items.why: Students know less energy is wasted and reach for resistance as the only obvious cause, since resistance is what wastes energy. Resistance depends on the cable itself, not on the supply. Identify the quantity that actually changes, which is the current.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do transformers make up for the energy wasted in the cables?
items.correct: No. Transformers change the potential difference; they do not create energy. They reduce the waste by allowing a smaller current.
items.misconception: Transformers add extra energy back into the system to replace what the cables waste.
items.why: Step-up sounds like a boost, and students picture the transformer topping the supply back up. A transformer changes potential difference and current together, keeping the power transferred essentially the same. Energy is never added.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the National Grid store electricity until consumers need it?
items.correct: No. The grid transfers electrical power from power stations to consumers; it is a transfer system, not a store.
items.misconception: Electricity is stored in the grid's cables, like water in a reservoir, and drawn out when an appliance is switched on.
items.why: The word grid suggests a reservoir or supply, and taps and reservoirs are the everyday model for anything piped to a house. Describe the grid as cables and transformers that carry power as it is generated, so demand must be matched by generation at the time.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two appliances are switched on for the same time. Do they transfer the same energy?
items.correct: Only if their powers are equal. In one minute a 900 W microwave transfers 54 000 J while a 60 W lamp transfers 3600 J.
items.misconception: If two appliances run for the same length of time they must transfer the same amount of energy.
items.why: Once the times match, students see only one variable left and assume the outcome must match too. Energy depends on the power as well as the time. Work out E = P t for each appliance separately and compare.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the energy transferred depend only on how long an appliance is on?
items.correct: No. It depends on how long the appliance is switched on for and on the power of the appliance.
items.misconception: The longer it is on, the more energy it transfers, so time alone decides the energy.
items.why: Time is the variable students can see changing, and 'leaving things on' is the everyday message about wasting energy. Both factors matter. Halving the power and doubling the time leaves the energy transferred unchanged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should the potential difference be stepped up everywhere in the National Grid?
items.correct: No. It is stepped up onto the transmission cables, then stepped down to a much lower value for domestic use.
items.misconception: Since a high potential difference is efficient, every transformer in the grid must step it up.
items.why: Students learn that a high pd reduces waste and apply that rule to the whole journey, without asking what pd a house actually needs. The high pd is only useful in the long transmission cables. Consumers need a much lower value, so the last transformer must step down.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: To find V from E = Q V, does it matter which way round you divide?
items.correct: Yes. V = E ÷ Q, so 540 J ÷ 45 C = 12 V. Dividing the other way gives 0.083, which is not a potential difference.
items.misconception: As long as you divide the two numbers given, you will get the right answer.
items.why: Students remember that a division is needed but rearrange by feel rather than by algebra, often dividing the smaller number by the larger. Rearrange the equation on paper first, then substitute. Checking units helps: joules ÷ coulombs gives volts, coulombs ÷ joules does not.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.2.4 Energy transfers
